items.title: When the Academie was founded
items.claim: The Academie francaise was established to regulate the French language. In which year and under whose authority?
items.reveal:
Richelieu gave letters patent on 29 January 1635. The Academie has 40 'immortels' and has been working on its Dictionnaire since 1694 (first edition).

The ninth edition has been in progress since 1986 and was completed in 2024.
items.why: Language regulation in France is a centuries-long state project, not a recent reaction to globalisation.

items.title: Languages spoken in France in 1789
items.claim: Abbe Gregoire's 1794 report estimated what proportion of French citizens spoke standard French as a native language at the time of the Revolution?
items.reveal_title: A small minority spoke standard French
items.reveal:
Gregoire's report 'Rapport sur la necessite et les moyens d'aneantir les patois' estimated that only around 3 million of 25 million inhabitants spoke French well; many used Occitan, Breton, Alsatian, Basque or other languages.

Universal primary education in the late 19th century did much of the standardisation.
items.why: Modern national languages are often the product of policy as much as organic spread.

items.title: When Beauvoir's Le Deuxieme Sexe appeared
items.claim: Simone de Beauvoir's Le Deuxieme Sexe was published in which year?
items.reveal:
The book contains the often-cited line 'On ne nait pas femme: on le devient' ('One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman').

The Vatican placed it on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1956.
items.why: A single publication can crystallise a long intellectual movement and trigger immediate institutional reaction.

items.title: Camus and Nobel age
items.claim: When Albert Camus won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957, he was the second-youngest laureate at the time. About what age?
items.reveal:
Camus published L'Etranger in 1942 and La Peste in 1947. He died in a car accident on 4 January 1960.

Rudyard Kipling at 41 was younger when he won in 1907.
items.why: Award timing is shaped by the political and editorial currents of its decade.

items.title: Where most French speakers will live
items.claim: OIF (Observatoire de la langue francaise) projections suggest that by 2050, roughly what share of French speakers will live in Africa?
items.reveal_title: Most French speakers will be African
items.reveal:
OIF estimates (Demographie et langue francaise reports) project that demographic growth in francophone Africa will lift the African share of French speakers to around 85% by 2050.

This follows from population growth in countries such as DR Congo, where French is an official or working language.
items.why: The geographic centre of a language can shift dramatically across a generation.

items.title: Loi Toubon
items.claim: France's loi Toubon (1994) requires French in certain official contexts. Which is closest to what it covers?

options.text: It bans English speech in private homes
It requires French in commercial advertising, employment contracts and public-sector communication, with alternatives in foreign languages permitted but a French version also required
It applies only to government emails
It applies only to broadcast television

items.reveal_title: It mandates French in public commercial and administrative contexts
items.reveal:
The law was originally proposed by Jacques Toubon (then Minister of Culture). Some clauses were softened by the Constitutional Council on freedom-of-expression grounds.

Enforcement is sporadic but has produced occasional fines.
items.why: Language policy is most visible at the interface between commerce and state.

items.title: What the Academie recommends instead of 'email'
items.claim: The Academie francaise has recommended a French alternative to 'email'. What is it?
items.reveal:
Quebec coined 'courriel' first; the Academie endorsed it in 2003. Similar recommendations include 'mot-diese' (hashtag) and 'jeu video en nuage' (cloud gaming).

Usage in France varies; 'mail' and 'email' remain common in practice.
items.why: Official terminology and everyday usage often diverge, sometimes lastingly.

items.title: What the passe compose replaced
items.claim: In modern spoken French, the passe compose has largely replaced which other tense?
items.reveal_title: Passe simple has retreated to formal writing
items.reveal:
Spoken French uses the passe compose where 19th-century literature used the passe simple. The simple form survives in formal narrative writing, historical writing, and some regional usage.

The shift has been described in detail by linguists since at least Damourette and Pichon (1911-1936).
items.why: Grammatical structures can fall out of speech but persist in writing for generations.

items.title: Subjunctive use today
items.claim: The imparfait du subjonctif is widely described as moribund in modern French. In what context might it still appear?

options.text: In very formal literary writing, often for stylistic effect

items.reveal:
The form survives in writing for archaic or formal register. Spoken French typically uses the present subjunctive where the imperfect would be classical.

Grevisse's Le Bon Usage remains a standard reference describing the changing patterns.
items.why: Grammatical change is often gradual, leaving an archaic register that signals formality.

items.title: Origin of the term 'franglais'
items.claim: The term 'franglais' was popularised by a 1964 book. Who wrote it?
items.reveal_title: Etiemble's 1964 polemic gave the term wide circulation
items.reveal:
Etiemble argued anglicisms were displacing French vocabulary and weakening the language. The debate continues in different forms; OQLF in Quebec polices anglicisms more strictly than France.

Great numbers of English loans have nonetheless entered French dictionaries since.
items.why: Concerns about language change recur in similar form across generations.

items.title: When 'iel' entered Le Robert
items.claim: Le Robert added the gender-neutral pronoun 'iel' (combining il and elle) to its online edition in which year?
items.reveal:
The inclusion drew commentary from the Education Minister and politicians. The Academie francaise has been sceptical of inclusive writing more broadly.

Dictionaries describe usage rather than prescribe it.
items.why: Dictionary inclusions of contested terms become flashpoints in language politics.

items.title: France and minority languages
items.claim: Which European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages instrument has France signed but not yet ratified?

options.text: France signed in 1999 but has not ratified, citing constitutional issues

items.reveal:
The 1958 Constitution's Article 2 declares 'la langue de la Republique est le francais', cited as an obstacle to ratification.

A 2021 law strengthening regional language teaching was partially overturned by the Constitutional Council.
items.why: Constitutional commitments to a single official language can constrain participation in international minority-language frameworks.
